intro.kicker: Get Bromic · Brand campaign concept · US and Australia
intro.headline: Every Ad In This Category Looks The Same
lines: Golden hour, an infinity pool, a cashmere throw and two glasses of wine nobody drinks. Swap the logo at the end and the same film could run for any outdoor heating brand.
When an ad could belong to anyone, the money behind it builds the whole category and does little for Bromic.
Outdoor heating is bought once, considered slowly and often decided at a showroom counter. Get Bromic is built to make Bromic the name people remember when they reach that counter.
In the agency's review, humor is the one register no brand in the category has claimed. Get Bromic uses it, and the warmth turns on in every frame.

argument.headline: Keep The Promise. Add The Argument.
body: Extend The Moment stays. It is Bromic's promise, it is what our heaters deliver, and it is where every film in this platform resolves.
A promise on its own rarely creates urgency. It asks people to want more of an evening that is already pleasant, which is why outdoor heating so often moves to next year's budget.
So the campaign adds an argument beneath the promise. Your outdoor room is an investment you have already made, and every cold evening it sits empty is part of that investment going unused.

That moves the decision away from a heater price-shopped against a hardware-store mushroom and places it beside the pergola, the outdoor kitchen and the pool, where heating is one of the smallest lines on the budget.
It is also the version of the argument that speaks to an architect. An unheated outdoor room is designed square footage the client cannot use for much of the year, and clients remember who drew it.
argument.pull_quote: You didn't spend eighty thousand dollars on a backyard to look at it through glass.

filter.headline: Every Joke Has To Be A Bromic Joke

pass.title: Jokes About The Space Going Unused
pass.body: The backyard that sits empty after dark, or the pizza oven fired four times a year. Only a premium, built-in, specified brand can tell these jokes, and each one makes the case for the investment while it gets the laugh.

fail.title: Jokes About Being Cold
fail.body: Chattering teeth and piles of blankets are funny, and any heater brand could run them. They also cast heat as a remedy for discomfort, which is a commodity job sold at a commodity price.

filter.test: If the joke would still work for a cheap hardware-store heater, cut it, or rewrite the caption so it lands on the space that goes unused. Concepts tagged COLD need that caption work before production.

format.headline: One Cut, From Cold To Warm
format.body: Each film holds a cold, quietly absurd scene with a straight face for about twenty-five seconds. Then the heat comes on, the light warms and the space fills with people. Select Get Bromic on any frame to see the turn.
beats: The Bromic heater is in frame, unlit, and the brand appears within three seconds.
A deadpan escalation in one location, played straight.
The heater comes on with the Bromic sound cue and a warm amber glow, and the Affinity Smart-Heat® control that turns it on is in shot.
Get Bromic, the logo and the URL.
format.rule: Funny advertising often fails on attribution: people remember the joke and forget the brand. So every cut, including the six-second version, carries the brand in the first three seconds and at the end, shows a real Bromic heater and its control during the turn, and uses the same sound cue.

films_intro.headline: One Shoot For Both Markets
films_intro.body: These six films cover both hemispheres, the three homeowner segments and the trade, and each turn carries one product truth from the Tungsten Smart-Heat® Electric Series II framework, with its Affinity Smart-Heat® control. Four of them switch between the US and Australia with a single supered card. The mood frames are AI-generated direction for light, staging and casting; they show no real Bromic product, and production films real Bromic heaters installed exactly as the manuals specify. Every price in the films is illustrative and must be replaced with verified local pricing before it runs.

receipts_intro.headline: The Receipt
body: An itemized list of what the outdoor room cost, line by line, and then one final line: the warmth that lets you use it, and the smallest number on the list.

The films build recognition and the receipts make the case in numbers. A receipt is pure typography, quick and inexpensive to produce, and it re-prices for a homeowner, a builder or a venue operator by changing the line items. It also works well on a dealer counter card.
Every figure on these receipts is illustrative. Each one must be replaced with verified local pricing, signed off by Finance and Sales operations, before anything runs.
receipts_intro.legal: The itemized price list is a common device. The sign-off of Mastercard's long-running campaign is a registered trademark the company protects closely, so never use its final word, its voiceover rhythm, its type treatment or its card imagery. Our receipt ends on something you can buy, which helps, and legal counsel must still clear the final wording before production.

scenes_intro.headline: Price The Whole Space, Then The Warmth
scenes_intro.body: Each object in the photograph wears a price tag, and the total climbs as you look. The last tag lands on the heating, the one thing nobody priced, and it is the smallest number in the frame. Tags are set as live type over the photograph, never baked into an image, so one plate re-prices for a market, a currency or a specification in minutes. Every figure is illustrative and must be replaced with verified local pricing before it runs, and the final plates are real photographs of Bromic heaters installed correctly.

concepts_intro.headline: Thirty-Two Ideas, Each Read Four Ways
concepts_intro.body: Twenty-three concepts work unchanged in both markets. Six are twins with a local version, often one word or one place card apart; two are native to Australia and one to the US. Every concept carries four readings, Deadpan, Dry, Absurd and Dark, so you can judge it in each register. Concepts tagged COLD need their caption reworked onto the unused space before production, and those tagged R-MED or R-HI are tested first. The seasons run opposite in each hemisphere, so one production can run from August to November in the US and from February to May in Australia.

trade_intro.headline: The Same Platform, In Their Terms
body: The homeowner films are about a backyard that goes unused. Builders and venue operators measure something else: for a builder, reputation, callbacks and referrals; for an operator, covers, reviews and labor. The endline, the art direction and the straight face stay the same, and the story moves into their world.

These run in the Deadpan or Dry register only, never Absurd or Dark. A restaurateur ordering forty heaters does not want jokes about being cold, and a builder does not want to be the punchline in front of a client. Each one should make the audience think that has happened to me.

tiers.headline: Homeowners, 40 To 70
rows: Remodeling, adding on, and buying or building new.
Make Bromic the name they ask for at the showroom counter.

Reach people before heating occurs to them: renovation and custom-build intent, recent movers into high-value homes, outdoor kitchen and pool audiences, premium appliance interests, design-magazine readers and lookalikes built from the dealer CRM. Searches for patio heaters are a small, price-led pool.

Meta feed and Reels (9:16 first), YouTube and connected TV, where a 30-second film with real production values gets watched; Pinterest and Houzz for stills. The agency believes this audience watches more connected TV than average, and Digital marketing confirms it with platform data before media is bought.

Places with a real cold season and high home values: the Northeast, the Mid-Atlantic, Chicago, the Mountain states, the Pacific Northwest and coastal California. In Australia, Melbourne, Sydney, Adelaide and coastal New South Wales and Victoria.
August to November in the US and February to May in Australia.

tiers.headline: Architects, Designers, Builders And Commercial
rows: Get Bromic onto the drawing and into the specification.

The same endline and art direction, with the detail up front: coverage, mounting and recess details, the Affinity Smart-Heat® Controls that come with every heater, Tungsten Coastal for life by the water, the warranty and continuing-education courses.
LinkedIn, trade press, ArchDaily, showroom and dealer co-op, and rep visits.
January to March, when renovation planning and specification work happen.
The Specification (film 06) is the humorous trade film. The client's question lands on the specifier's reputation, which is what moves this audience.

sections.dealer: Outdoor heating often closes at a counter, with a person. Budget for co-branded cutdowns, in-store stills, a showroom badge and a one-page sales sheet built on the argument: heating is a small share of what the outdoor room cost, and it decides whether the room is used for most of the year or for a few months of it. The deck's own figures for that sheet are agency estimates and stay off it until verified.

measurement.headline: Measure Whether People Remember Bromic
rows: Branded search volume for Bromic, the quickest and cleanest read. Set the baseline now.
Unaided and aided awareness in the target audience, before and after.
One tracked field in the dealer portal, “customer asked for Bromic by name.”
A matched-market test with six markets live and six held out, read through dealer sell-through. The agency recommends it as the most credible evidence of return for a brand campaign.
Three-second views, ThruPlays and completion rate. Watch them, and never optimize the films toward them.
Click-through rate, cost per click and cost per lead on the brand films.
measurement.warning: Agree this in writing before launch. Brand campaigns are often cut when an early dashboard shows a low click-through rate and the budget moves to retargeting. The agency recommends roughly 60% brand and 40% conversion activity in year one, so the demand the films create has somewhere to land; the split is the agency's recommendation, for Digital marketing and Leadership to set.

rows.title: Attribution
rows.text: People remember the joke and forget the brand. The brand appears in the first three seconds and at the end, the real product and its control are in the turn, and one sound cue and one voice run across every film.

rows.title: Losing The Specifiers
rows.text: Architects and designers judge the craft. Hold it to a luxury standard with cinema lenses, real houses and real light, and keep the comedy in the writing. Show the work to eight to ten partner firms before launch so they feel consulted.

rows.title: Products Shown Wrongly
rows.text: The mood frames show generic heaters. Production films real Bromic heaters, mounted, cleared and controlled exactly as the manuals specify, and every frame is checked by the Product team.

rows.title: Unverified Numbers
rows.text: Every price and figure in the platform is illustrative. Each is replaced with verified local pricing, and every arithmetic line is checked, before anything runs.

rows.title: Drifting Down-Market
rows.text: Apply the discipline filter in every round of review.

rows.title: Intellectual Property
rows.text: Never name, quote or recreate a film, TV show, sports event or campaign, and never use a recognizable score. No animal is ever shown in distress. Legal counsel reviews every parody concept before production.

rows.title: A Competitor Responds
rows.text: Expect a price or made-locally response. One product truth in every turn gives the humor a reason to believe.

rows.title: The Wrong Tone For Venues
rows.text: A restaurateur ordering forty heaters does not want jokes about being cold, so the trade tier runs Deadpan or Dry.

films.title: The Mushroom
films.line: Seventy thousand dollars of outdoor kitchen. Heated by an eighty-nine dollar mushroom.
films.story: A $70,000 outdoor kitchen, and in the middle of it one cheap mushroom heater standing like a traffic cone. Three adults press shoulder to shoulder inside its small circle of warmth while the kitchen, the twelve-seat table and the built-in sofa sit empty around them.
films.why: Our lead recommendation, because one frame carries both the joke and the price argument. A big-box hardware-store mushroom heater reads instantly in both markets, so the retailer never needs naming.
tones: Seventy thousand dollars of outdoor kitchen. Heated by an eighty-nine dollar mushroom.
The kitchen was designed by an architect. The heating was decided in aisle twelve.
They own a pizza oven, a wine fridge and a built-in griddle. They are standing in a circle around a lamp.
Somewhere in this photograph is a man who spent his bonus on this.
films.turn: Tungsten Smart-Heat® Electric, recessed flush in the kitchen ceiling, dimmed up on the Affinity Smart-Heat® Dimmer Controller as the mushroom goes dark.
films.proof: The worry-free, dual fan-ventilated low-clearance recess sits flush in a 7.5 in ceiling cavity, with the recess box supplied in the kit and nothing to build on site.

films.title: The Pizza Oven
films.story: A $9,000 wood-fired oven. He fires it, tends it and slides out a beautiful pizza. Everyone takes a slice and heads inside, and he stands alone in the dark in a puffer jacket, holding the peel, beside the most expensive appliance he has ever bought.
films.why: Pizza ovens are everywhere in both markets, so the scene is recognized instantly and needs no translation.
tones: Four times a year.
Nine thousand dollars. Roughly two thousand two hundred a pizza.
He has built a brick monument to a food he eats indoors.
He fires it up so he has a reason to stand outside alone.
films.turn: Tungsten Smart-Heat® Electric on the pergola beside the oven, dimmed up on the Affinity Smart-Heat® Dimmer Controller as the guests drift back out.
films.proof: Dual elements on the 4 and 6 kW models deliver up to 6 kW of directional warmth, turned up on a cold night and down on a mild one with the Affinity Smart-Heat® Dimmer.

films.title: The Snowbirds / The Queensland Run
films.line: The Wilsons solved their outdoor heating problem. It cost four hundred thousand dollars.
films.story: A retired couple planned their whole retirement around the terrace. Instead, every year, they pack the car, drive to a second home somewhere warm and stay for five months. Cut to the second property.
films.why: Snowbirds in the US and the winter run to Queensland in Australia are the same habit, so one film serves both markets with a different destination plate. It is the most extreme version of the price argument, and it should land hardest with people aged 55 to 70.
tones: The Wilsons solved their outdoor heating problem. It cost four hundred thousand dollars.
There is a cheaper way to spend five months somewhere warm.
They drive eleven hundred miles a year to sit outside. They own an outside.
They bought a second house rather than have the conversation.
films.turn: Tungsten Smart-Heat® Electric on the terrace wall, switched on to a schedule in the Bromic app through the Affinity Smart-Heat® Dimmer Controller, so the terrace is already warm when they step outside.
films.proof: Schedules and timers in the Bromic app, with Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant voice control, through compatible Affinity Smart-Heat® Controls sold separately.

films.title: The Big Game / Finals Day
films.line: The outdoor TV cost six thousand dollars. Everyone is watching the small one.
films.story: Twenty-two people crammed into a living room around a modest screen. Push through the glass behind them to the outdoor lounge, the bar and its own 85-inch television, dark and dry under the roof and completely empty.
films.why: The US version plays on the championship weekend in February and the Australian version on football finals day in September. It is one shot in opposite months, shipped to both markets with a single supered date card. Name neither event nor league, because both are protected trademarks.
tones: The outdoor TV cost six thousand dollars. Everyone is watching the small one.
Twenty-two people. One bathroom. An empty terrace nine feet away.
There is an eighty-five inch television outside, broadcasting to four garden chairs and a moth.
The outdoor television has never seen a human face.
films.turn: Tungsten Smart-Heat® Electric on the lounge ceiling, aimed at the sofas and dimmed up on the Affinity Smart-Heat® Dimmer Controller as the crowd moves outside.
films.proof: Tungsten mounts on flat or pitched ceilings, on walls or on an extended wall bracket, and angles to aim its warmth at the seating.

films.title: The Coastal Breeze
films.line: Built for the view. Emptied by the breeze.
films.story: The beach house is flawless. Every evening at five past five the sea breeze arrives and the deck empties in under a minute, plates lifted, napkins gone and everyone inside. Time-lapsed across a week until it becomes a rhythm.
films.why: The film that carries Tungsten Coastal. It is built for life by the water, and radiant heat warms people and surfaces directly, so it holds up in a light sea breeze where warmed air simply drifts away. Shoot it in Byron Bay or on the Mornington Peninsula in Australia, and on Cape Cod, in the Hamptons or on the California coast in the US, and show it to architects.
tones: Built for the view. Emptied by the breeze.
The architect solved the light, the sightlines and the wind. Two out of three.
Every evening at five past five, the ocean asks everyone to leave.
They paid for the view. They watch it through glass, like everyone else.
films.turn: Tungsten Smart-Heat® Electric Coastal under the deck roof, dimmed up on the Affinity Smart-Heat® Dimmer Controller as the breeze comes in.
films.proof: Tungsten Coastal protects against corrosion twice over, with a marine-grade 316 stainless build and a high-temperature, corrosion-resistant coating, for coastal homes and venues.

films.title: The Specification
films.line: The space is specified. Now specify the season.
films.story: An architect presents a beautiful render, all golden light, people and wine. The client studies it, then points. “And in November?” (In Australia, “And in July?”) The architect opens their mouth and nothing comes out. Hold on it.
films.why: The trade workhorse, for LinkedIn, the trade press and the rep's leave-behind. It keeps the endline and places the client's question on the specifier's reputation, which is what moves this audience. The call to action is the specification kit.
tones: The space is specified. Now specify the season.
The render never has weather in it.
The render has eleven people in it. November has none.
The client will remember who drew it.
films.turn: Tungsten Smart-Heat® Electric Series II in the render, recessed and post-mounted across the terrace, zoned on Affinity Smart-Heat® Dimmer Controllers.
films.proof: A single post replaces the two-post mount of Series I, and recessing needs no box built on site, with one low-clearance kit across Select and Coastal.
films.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

tones: “Still on for tonight?” · “Yes. Though it’s meant to drop to nine.” · “…indoors?” · “Indoors 👍”
Four messages. The same four messages, since March.
The terrace has its own group chat. It has never been invited.
Nobody suggests outside any more. They stopped a while ago.
concepts.production: Motion graphics only, with no shoot. Useful as always-on social between film flights, and the dates refresh each season for new creative at almost no cost.
concepts.local: Australia keeps nine (°C); the US version reads forty-eight (°F). Flip the month by hemisphere. That is the entire localization.

concepts.title: The Open Home / The Listing Photo
concepts.caption: “Seamless indoor-outdoor living.”
concepts.story: The agent stages the outdoor kitchen for the listing shoot. The shutter clicks and everyone sprints inside. It speaks to people buying or selling a home, a moment heating brands rarely address.
tones: “Seamless indoor-outdoor living.”
Photographed in use. Sold on a promise. Used in March.
The prosecco in the listing photo has been there since 2023.
The photograph is the only time anyone sat there.
concepts.audience: People buying or selling a home
concepts.production: A strong dealer and showroom piece, because it matches a moment agents and builders already talk about.
concepts.local: US: the online listing photo. Australia: the Saturday open home. Name no listing site.

concepts.title: It's Not That Cold / She'll Be Right
concepts.caption: “It's actually really nice out here.” / “She'll be right.”
concepts.story: Dad, alone at his own party in a beanie on the good furniture, insisting it is lovely. A COLD concept, so the turn has to land on the furniture finally being used.
tones: “It’s actually really nice out here.” / “She’ll be right.”
He is the only guest at his own party.
He has been out there for forty minutes. He will not be broken.
He is proving something. Nobody is sure what.
concepts.audience: Family decision-makers; the partner who is not the enthusiast
concepts.production: A COLD concept. The turn must land on the furniture coming back into use, with the warmth as the reason, or it pulls the brand down-market.
concepts.local: US: “It's actually really nice out here.” Australia: “She'll be right.” One line changes.

concepts.title: Melbourne
concepts.caption: Melbourne.
concepts.story: One dinner party through four complete weather cycles, layers on and off in a rising rhythm, and nobody mentions it.
tones: Melbourne.
Four seasons. One dinner.
By dessert they had removed and replaced every item of clothing they own.
They stopped commenting on it years ago.
concepts.production: A rhythm piece where the comedy lives in the edit. Inexpensive to shoot, at one table in one afternoon.
concepts.local: Native to Melbourne. Transfers to Denver, Chicago or San Francisco with a city card.

concepts.title: Alfresco (n.)
concepts.caption: Alfresco (n.). Italian, “in the open air.” Australian, “the bit near the barbecue nobody uses after May.”
concepts.story: Native to Australia, where alfresco is a specific, everyday word in home building. The US twin runs as “Pergola (n.): a structure for looking at.”
tones: Alfresco (n.). Italian, “in the open air.” Australian, “the bit near the barbecue nobody uses after May.”
An Italian word for an Australian room nobody enters.
Alfresco: a large outdoor space for storing a barbecue you are not using.
It’s in the brochure and in the photos. It’s missing from most of the year.
concepts.production: Set in Bromic's typography at large size. The tension between the beautiful photograph and the blunt caption is the joke.
concepts.local: Australia only. The US twin runs as “Pergola (n.): a structure for looking at.”

concepts.title: Labor Day / Easter: The Closing Ceremony
concepts.caption: The Petersons observe the end of summer. It is seventy-eight degrees.
concepts.story: A family solemnly closes the pool, folds the umbrellas and wheels the grill away, shot like a funeral. The weather is still perfect.
tones: The Petersons observe the end of summer. It is seventy-eight degrees.
The pool closes by the calendar. The weather was never consulted.
They have folded the umbrellas in perfect silence. One of them is crying.
Nothing has ended. They’ve just decided it has.
concepts.production: Shot like a funeral and played entirely straight. Hold on a thermometer or a supered temperature so the perfect weather is clear.
concepts.local: US: Labor Day, seventy-eight degrees (°F). Australia: Easter, twenty-six degrees (°C). The same ceremony on a different date card.

concepts.title: The Big Game / Finals Day
concepts.caption: The outdoor TV cost six thousand dollars. Everyone is watching the small one.
concepts.story: Twenty-two people crammed inside while the outdoor lounge and its own 85-inch screen sit dark and dry. February in the US, September in Australia, one film and one date card.
tones: The outdoor TV cost six thousand dollars. Everyone is watching the small one.
Twenty-two people. One bathroom. An empty terrace nine feet away.
There is an eighty-five inch television outside, broadcasting to four garden chairs and a moth.
The outdoor television has never seen a human face.
concepts.audience: Households that have already built an outdoor room
concepts.production: One film for both markets, with a single supered date card: the same shot in the opposite month.
concepts.local: US: the championship game in February. Australia: football finals day in September. Name neither event nor league; both are protected trademarks.

concepts.title: The Housewarming
concepts.caption: You should not need equipment to attend a dinner party.
concepts.story: The invitation said “dress warm.” Twenty adults in ski jackets and beanies over evening clothes, holding champagne in an award-winning garden, and nobody mentions it.
tones: You should not need equipment to attend a dinner party.
Black tie. Thermal base layer.
Twenty adults in ski jackets holding champagne in an award-winning garden. Nobody mentions it.
Everyone is having a lovely time and everyone is lying.
concepts.audience: New-build owners and the design-conscious decision maker
concepts.production: A STATUS concept: the quiet embarrassment of a beautiful thing that does not work, which is the emotional core of the platform. Wardrobe does all the work.
concepts.local: None.

concepts.title: The Year After
concepts.caption: “And how are you finding the terrace?”
concepts.story: The follow-up interview, twelve months on, and a very long silence. Aimed at the trade, because the unused terrace reflects on the people who designed it.
tones: “And how are you finding the terrace?”
The pause is the answer.
The silence lasted long enough that the crew stopped filming.
It’s the best thing they built and the least thing they use.
concepts.production: Makes a specifier usefully uncomfortable. Use a generic home-build documentary format with no program title, format or presenter likeness, and have legal counsel review it.
concepts.local: Works in both markets as a generic home-build documentary. Name no program.
concepts.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

concepts.title: The Specification
concepts.caption: The space is specified. Now specify the season.
concepts.story: “And in November?” The architect has no answer. The trade workhorse.
tones: The space is specified. Now specify the season.
The render never has weather in it.
The render has eleven people in it. November has none.
The client will remember who drew it.
concepts.audience: Architects, designers, custom builders, commercial specifiers
concepts.production: It keeps the endline and places the client's question on the specifier's reputation, the currency that moves this audience. The call to action is the specification kit, kept apart from the joke.
concepts.local: US: “And in November?” Australia: “And in July?”
concepts.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

concepts.title: Two Hours
concepts.caption: Your terrace has an opening time and a closing time. You never agreed to either.
concepts.story: A locked-off time-lapse: 4 pm full, 6 pm half, 7 pm one abandoned drink. Persuasive for anyone close to buying, because the argument arrives inside the joke.
tones: Your terrace has an opening time and a closing time. You never agreed to either.
Four o’clock: twelve people. Seven o’clock: one abandoned drink.
The terrace is open from four until six. It sets its own hours.
Nobody decides to go in. They just find themselves inside.
concepts.audience: Active considerers already aware of the brand
concepts.production: Run it behind the funnier films as the consideration layer, for people who already know Bromic.
concepts.local: None.

concepts.title: The Kids' Table
concepts.caption: There is a better solution.
concepts.story: Thanksgiving. The kids' table has been put outside, and one child holds unbroken eye contact with the camera. Dark, so it needs a warm turn or it reads as mean.
tones: There is a better solution.
The overflow seating is outside. It is November.
Four children eating Thanksgiving dinner in coats, maintaining eye contact through the glass.
They will remember this one.
concepts.production: The turn brings the table back into the party. Test it with the audience before committing (R-HI).
concepts.local: Native to the US Thanksgiving. Do not force an Australian version.

concepts.title: The Deck
concepts.caption: Beautifully maintained. Entirely unused.
concepts.story: He oils and polishes the deck the way other men polish a car, steps back, admires it and goes inside. Deck pride is the same in both countries.
tones: Beautifully maintained. Entirely unused.
He oils it twice a year. He sits on it twice a year. Never the same day.
The deck has a skincare routine.
He visits it on weekends, like a relative.
concepts.production: Play it tenderly. The affection for the deck is real, and the audience shares it.
concepts.local: None.

concepts.title: The Hostage Negotiation
concepts.caption: Negotiations broke down at 7:40pm.
concepts.story: Guests barricaded in the kitchen, wrapped in blankets. Outside, crouched behind the unused outdoor sofa, a man with a megaphone and a clipboard. “They say they'll come out if there are blankets. There are no more blankets, Gary.”
tones: Negotiations broke down at 7:40pm.
Fifteen guests, one terrace, and nobody willing to cross nine feet of cold.
There are no more blankets, Gary.
They have everything they need in there. They are never coming out.
concepts.production: The funniest concept in the bank and the hardest to pitch on paper. Play it with complete tactical seriousness, because one wink kills it. Cast a character actor for the negotiator, and keep it clear of any real incident or recognizable film. Gary is a fictional character.
concepts.local: None. The standoff reads the same in both markets.

concepts.title: Rusty
concepts.caption: Rusty is the only member of this family getting any value from the outdoor kitchen.
concepts.story: A slow, loving portrait of a dog asleep in the very center of an $84,000 outdoor lounge. Nobody else is there, and nobody has been since March.
tones: Rusty is the only member of this family getting any value from the outdoor kitchen.
Eighty-four thousand dollars, enjoyed exclusively by the dog.
The dog has sole possession of the entertaining area and shows no sign of sharing it.
He waits out there every evening. Nobody has joined him since March.
concepts.production: Warm and affectionate, which is what lets it travel; the agency sees it as the most shareable piece. Cast the dog first, and everything else is set dressing.
concepts.local: Flip the month by hemisphere.

concepts.title: The Safety Briefing
concepts.caption: “Tonight's outdoor portion of the evening is expected to last approximately eleven minutes.”
concepts.story: A host briefs the dinner guests like cabin crew, covering layers, exits and the location of the blankets. The guests listen politely, and one takes notes.
tones: “Tonight's outdoor portion of the evening is expected to last approximately eleven minutes.”
Layers. Exits. The location of the blankets.
One of the guests is taking notes.
Everyone has done this before. That is what makes it sad.
concepts.production: The least expensive of the three lead concepts to shoot, with one location, one performance and eight extras. The comedy lives in the host's sincerity.
concepts.local: None.

concepts.title: The Valuation
concepts.caption: “And how often would you say you use it?” … “I'll put ‘as new’.”
concepts.story: An antiques valuer appraises the outdoor kitchen with a loupe while the owners stand beside him, visibly uncomfortable.
tones: “And how often would you say you use it?” … “I'll put ‘as new’.”
Forty-one thousand dollars, in showroom condition, four years on.
He has valued it twice. Both times as unused stock.
It will outlast them, unused, and be sold that way.
concepts.production: “As new” is the whole film. Cut anything that delays it.
concepts.local: The antiques-show register plays broader in Australia; the US plays it drier.

concepts.title: The Gym Membership
concepts.caption: Your gym membership is the second most expensive thing you own and don't use.
concepts.story: A single line over a still of an empty terrace at dusk. Anyone over forty understands it at once, and it reframes the purchase in one sentence.
tones: Your gym membership is the second most expensive thing you own and don't use.
The gym costs you eighty dollars a month. This one was eighty thousand, once.
You have a second living room and you visit it eleven times a year.
You already know which room this is about.
concepts.production: A strong line for billboards and outdoor, because it works with or without the picture. Set it large and alone.
concepts.local: None.

concepts.title: Missing Persons
concepts.caption: LAST SEEN: MARCH. IF YOU HAVE ANY INFORMATION…
concepts.story: A weathered poster stapled to a suburban lamppost. The photograph on it is a twelve-seat outdoor dining table.
tones: LAST SEEN: MARCH. IF YOU HAVE ANY INFORMATION…
Missing since March. Seats twelve. Answers to nothing.
Someone has put up posters for an outdoor dining table.
Nobody has reported it missing because nobody noticed.
concepts.production: Could also run as a real ambient stunt, with posters in affluent suburbs, subject to local permits. Set the poster type in post; never generate it.
concepts.local: Flip the month by hemisphere.

concepts.title: Support Group
concepts.caption: “Hi. I'm Dave. I've owned a wood-fired oven for four years.” … “Hi, Dave.”
concepts.story: A circle of plastic chairs in a community hall. Dave stands, holding a pizza peel. “I've used it eleven times.” Murmurs of recognition.
tones: “Hi. I'm Dave. I've owned a wood-fired oven for four years.” … “Hi, Dave.”
Eleven uses in four years. The room finds this unremarkable.
Every man in this circle owns something magnificent he cannot use.
Dave still defends the purchase. That is the part that worries them.
concepts.audience: Owners of one expensive outdoor thing
concepts.production: A sequel to The Pizza Oven. Keep the hall genuinely bleak, because the contrast with the warm Bromic world is the joke. Dave is fictional, and the meeting stays generic so it never mocks a real support program.
concepts.local: None.

concepts.title: Out of Office
concepts.caption: The terrace is currently out of office and will return in May.
concepts.story: An auto-reply from the terrace itself: “For urgent matters, please use the kitchen island.” Very low production cost and native to the feed.
tones: The terrace is currently out of office and will return in May.
For urgent matters, please use the kitchen island.
The terrace has set an auto-reply and stopped responding entirely.
It has been out of office longer than it has ever been in it.
concepts.production: Motion graphics only, with no shoot. Refresh the return date each season.
concepts.local: Flip the return month by hemisphere.

concepts.title: The Archaeologist
concepts.caption: “Evidence of a civilization that gathered outdoors, briefly, and only in February.”
concepts.story: Two archaeologists brush and measure around a suburban patio table with numbered markers, entirely straight-faced.
tones: “Evidence of a civilization that gathered outdoors, briefly, and only in February.”
The site shows heavy use across roughly six weeks, then nothing.
They have found a twelve-seat table and no evidence anyone sat at it.
Future generations will assume it was ceremonial.
concepts.production: Rated R-MED because the idea needs a beat to land. Play it as a straight natural-history documentary, with no comic music.
concepts.local: Flip the month by hemisphere.

concepts.title: The Reunion
concepts.caption: Nine months is a long time.
concepts.story: Spring. The furniture cover comes off in slow motion and the family greets the outdoor sofa like a relative home at last. Someone weeps.
tones: Nine months is a long time.
The cover comes off in September. It goes back on in March.
A grown adult is weeping at a sofa.
They are genuinely pleased to see it, and that is the problem.
concepts.production: A seasonal opener for the start of the outdoor season. The slow-motion reveal is the whole shot.
concepts.local: Flip the months: spring starts in March in the US and in September in Australia.

concepts.title: Couples Therapy
concepts.caption: “It's the pergola.”
concepts.story: Two people at opposite ends of a therapist's sofa. Neither will say it. Finally one does, and the therapist writes something down.
tones: “It's the pergola.”
Neither of them wanted to be the one to say it.
Forty minutes of silence, then one word: pergola.
They built it together. Neither has sat under it.
concepts.production: Rated R-MED. Keep it affectionate and never bitter, and have the therapist react as if this is completely normal.
concepts.local: None.

concepts.title: The Auction
concepts.caption: “Lot 42. Outdoor kitchen. One careful owner. Sixty-two hours' use.”
concepts.story: Gavel, catalog and spotlight. A complete built-in outdoor kitchen on a plinth in a formal auction house.
tones: “Lot 42. Outdoor kitchen. One careful owner. Sixty-two hours' use.”
Forty-one thousand new. Sixty-two hours used. Bidding starts at four.
It is being sold as an antiquity, which technically it is not.
It will be bought by someone who will also not use it.
concepts.production: The lot number and the hours-used figure do the work. Shoot it with real auction-house grandeur.
concepts.local: None.

trade.title: The Punch List
trade.caption: The last item on every punch list is the one you didn’t quote for.
trade.story: The final walkthrough. The client ticks down a clipboard on a flawless build, then writes one more line at the bottom: “Can we use it in winter?” Hold on the builder's face.
trade.insight: Many builders have been caught at handover by a question best answered at framing.
trade.argument: An unheated outdoor room leaves the job open. A finished build becomes an ongoing conversation, and that conversation costs the builder time nobody pays for.
trade.channels: LinkedIn, trade press, rep leave-behind, builder association newsletters.
trade.cta: Get the spec kit, with mounting, recess and rough-in details.
trade.audience: Custom home builders, remodelers, project managers
trade.production: Cast a real builder if you can, because this audience spots an actor at once. Shoot on a genuine near-complete site.
trade.kpi: Spec kit downloads and rep meetings booked.
tones: The last item on every punch list is the one you didn’t quote for.
Everything on the list was fixable. The last one wasn’t on the list.
He has signed off forty-one items. The forty-second is a season.
The build is finished. The conversation isn’t.
trade.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

trade.title: The Referral That Never Came
trade.caption: “Who built yours?” … “We love it. We’re inside a lot.”
trade.story: Two neighbors over a fence. The question every builder's business depends on gets asked, and the answer arrives one beat too late with one qualifier too many. The referral dies in the pause.
trade.insight: Custom builders rely heavily on word of mouth, and a lukewarm answer can do more harm than none at all.
trade.argument: An unused terrace rarely draws a complaint. It draws a hesitation, and a hesitation can quietly cost a builder the next job.
trade.channels: LinkedIn, trade press, dealer co-op, builder events.
trade.cta: Book a rep walkthrough on your next build.
trade.production: The whole film rests on one pause, so cast for timing. Shoot at golden hour so the unused terrace behind them reads clearly.
trade.kpi: Unaided builder awareness and rep meetings booked.
tones: “Who built yours?” … “We love it. We’re inside a lot.”
Nobody complained. Somebody hesitated.
Three seconds of silence over a fence just cost him his next job.
He’ll never know which job he lost, or why.
trade.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

trade.title: The Change Order
trade.caption: Rough it in now. Or cut it open later.
trade.story: A tradesperson cuts a neat rectangle into a beautiful finished cedar-lined ceiling to run a circuit. Sawdust falls onto new stone, and the homeowner watches, arms folded.
trade.insight: Adding outdoor heat after handover is costly and common, because the circuit was never roughed in.
trade.argument: Pre-wire during the build. It costs the client little at framing, and it gives the builder a defensible upgrade to put on the quote today.
trade.channels: LinkedIn, trade press, CEU content, rep leave-behind, dealer counter card.
trade.production: The trade piece most likely to convert, because it earns the builder money. Every electrical detail must be right, and the guide it points to carries the local-authority and licensed-electrician disclaimer; this audience will notice a wrong gauge or box.
trade.kpi: Rough-in guide downloads and the pre-wire attach rate reported by dealers.
tones: Rough it in now. Or cut it open later.
Four hundred dollars at framing. Six thousand after handover.
They are cutting a hole in a ceiling that took four days to line.
Everyone in this room knows exactly whose fault it is.
trade.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

trade.title: The Portfolio Shot
trade.caption: “Can we get one with people in it?”
trade.story: A photographer shoots the hero image for the builder's portfolio. The terrace is magnificent and completely empty. The builder asks for one with people in it, nobody moves, and the beat runs long.
trade.insight: The portfolio does much of a builder's marketing, and empty hero shots are an open secret in the trade.
trade.argument: An outdoor room that cannot be photographed in use is hard to sell to the next client. Heat becomes part of the builder's marketing as well as the client's comfort.
trade.channels: LinkedIn, Instagram to trade, ArchDaily, trade press.
trade.production: Ends on the photographer lowering the camera. Inexpensive to shoot with one location and three cast, and it pairs well with a reference-build series.
trade.kpi: Reference-build page visits and trade social engagement.
tones: “Can we get one with people in it?”
Every shot in the portfolio is empty. Nobody has asked why.
He has forty photographs of this house and no evidence anyone lives there.
The best work he’s ever done, and he can’t show it in use.
trade.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

trade.title: Six Hundred Square Feet
trade.caption: You sold them 4,200 square feet. You built them 4,800, for five months a year.
trade.story: A builder paces out a finished covered terrace at dusk, plans under one arm, gesturing across a beautiful empty space with the furniture still wrapped in plastic.
trade.insight: Builders sell square footage. An unheated outdoor room is square footage that sits idle for much of the year.
trade.argument: It speaks in the unit builders price in. Heating turns seasonal square footage into space the client can use for more of the year, at a small share of what the room cost to build.
trade.channels: LinkedIn, trade press, CEU, rep leave-behind, dealer sell sheet.
trade.cta: Run the numbers on your next build.
trade.production: Support it with a cost-per-square-foot comparison the rep can leave behind, built from verified figures and the Hub's sizing method. The film opens the conversation and the arithmetic closes it.
trade.kpi: Calculator use and attach rate on new builds.
tones: You sold them 4,200 square feet. You built them 4,800, for five months a year.
Six hundred square feet, seasonally available.
The most expensive room in the house has no walls and no year.
He charged for it, built it, and handed over something they can’t use.
trade.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

trade.title: The Completion Post
trade.caption: 340 likes. Nobody has stood in it since.
trade.story: A builder photographs his finished terrace at golden hour for social media. It is beautiful and completely empty. Cut to the same terrace in November, still empty.
trade.insight: The finished-project post matters to a custom builder's marketing, and it is almost always shot empty.
trade.argument: An outdoor room that photographs beautifully and cannot be used stays a portfolio picture. Heat is what turns the post into a referral.
trade.channels: LinkedIn, Instagram to trade, builder association channels.
trade.production: Self-aware enough that builders may share it themselves. Keep the post generic and never mimic a real platform's interface.
trade.kpi: Trade social engagement and reference-build page visits.
tones: 340 likes. Nobody has stood in it since.
Thrilled to announce the completion of a room nobody can enter in November.
The most photographed outdoor space in the county, and the least occupied.
The post did better than the terrace.
trade.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

trade.title: The Handover Pack
trade.caption: Appliance warranties. Paint codes. Maintenance schedules. “Terrace: see Spring.”
trade.story: A builder presents a beautiful leather-bound handover manual, with every system in the house documented. The client turns to the last page.
trade.insight: The handover pack is the last thing a builder controls and the first thing a client judges them by six months later.
trade.argument: Everything else in the house works on handover day. The terrace is the one room delivered with a season attached, and the one the builder will hear about again.
trade.channels: LinkedIn, trade press, rep leave-behind, builder association newsletters.
trade.cta: Add heat to your handover spec.
trade.production: Pairs with The Punch List as a two-film set. The manual should look genuinely expensive.
trade.kpi: Spec kit downloads and rep meetings booked.
tones: Appliance warranties. Paint codes. Maintenance schedules. “Terrace: see Spring.”
Every system in the house documented, except the one with no season.
The handover pack has a page for the terrace and it says “later”.
He has handed over a room he knows they cannot use.
trade.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

trade.title: Forty Covers
trade.caption: Forty covers. Closed for the season.
trade.story: A beautifully set restaurant terrace, roped off, cold and dark. The camera tracks past it to the packed golden interior and the line of people waiting by the door.
trade.insight: Every hospitality operator knows their cover count and revenue per cover to the dollar.
trade.argument: Heating the terrace adds capacity. Forty covers, times average spend, times the nights you cannot sell them today, gives a payback you can show on one slide.
trade.channels: Trade press, LinkedIn, hospitality trade shows, distributor and rep channels.
trade.cta: Get the payback calculation for your venue.
trade.audience: Restaurant, bar and hotel owners and operators
trade.production: Lead the commercial tier with this. The supered arithmetic at the end does more work than the film, so keep it accurate, conservative and built from the venue's own numbers in the Hub's payback calculator.
trade.kpi: Payback calculator completions and commercial quote requests.
tones: Forty covers. Closed for the season.
The waiting list is inside. The empty seats are outside.
There are twenty people in line nine feet from forty empty chairs.
He turns people away every night while looking at the seats.
trade.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

trade.title: The Two-Star Review
trade.caption: Your terrace is writing your reviews.
trade.story: An owner alone at the bar after close, lit by a tablet. On it: “Beautiful food. Sat outside. Couldn't feel my hands. ★★”
trade.insight: Operators feel reviews keenly, and a cold terrace can produce poor ones every shoulder season.
trade.argument: An unheated terrace costs the seats left empty, and it costs the seats you did fill on a cold night, along with the public review they leave behind.
trade.production: Rated R-MED. Never show a real review platform's branding or a real venue's name; design the interface from scratch, and have legal counsel review the review copy.
tones: Your terrace is writing your reviews.
Beautiful food. Two stars. The kitchen did nothing wrong.
A chef’s twenty-year career, reviewed by the weather.
It’ll be the first thing anyone reads about him for a year.
trade.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

trade.title: The Meteorologist
trade.caption: Your booking calendar should not have a meteorologist.
trade.story: Four in the afternoon. An events manager stands in a beautiful empty courtyard set for sixty, refreshing a weather app, then makes the call that cancels the booking. Repeated across a season.
trade.insight: Weather cancellations are a cost many venues absorb quietly, and few brands speak to it.
trade.argument: A venue that can rely on its outdoor space can sell it in advance and stop refunding it.
trade.channels: Trade press, LinkedIn, events and venue associations, wedding and functions trade.
trade.audience: Hotels, function centers, event venues, wedding venues
trade.production: Functions and weddings are a high-value, weather-exposed part of the commercial market. Consider a dedicated cut for that trade.
trade.kpi: Venue specification guide downloads and functions-sector quotes.
tones: Your booking calendar should not have a meteorologist.
Sixty covers, confirmed and paid. Cancelled at four o’clock by a forecast.
The most powerful person in this venue is a weather app.
She makes the call every time, and every time it costs her the same.
trade.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

trade.title: The Heater Graveyard
trade.caption: Ten years of solving it. Ten thousand dollars of not solving it.
trade.story: A back-of-house storeroom crammed with fifteen mismatched, dented, rusting mushroom heaters and gas bottles, the archaeology of a decade of quick fixes. The camera tracks along the row like a museum exhibit.
trade.insight: Many venues have this room, and few have added up what is in it.
trade.argument: Total cost of ownership is the argument that wins procurement. Replacing portable heaters season after season can cost more over ten years than installing permanent heaters once, before you count the gas, the storage and the labor, and the Hub's ten-year cost tool runs the comparison on the venue's own figures.
trade.channels: Trade press, LinkedIn, procurement and facilities channels, distributor reps.
trade.audience: Operators, facilities and procurement managers, hotel groups
trade.production: Find a genuinely grim real storeroom, with the venue's permission, because the comedy depends on it being real. Strongest for multi-site groups, where every figure multiplies by venue.
trade.kpi: Ten-year cost one-pager downloads and multi-site enquiries.
tones: Ten years of solving it. Ten thousand dollars of not solving it.
Fifteen heaters. Not one worked well enough to stop them buying the next.
A storeroom containing a decade of decisions, all of them the same decision.
Every one of these was going to be the one that fixed it.
trade.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.

trade.title: Four Hours a Week
trade.caption: Four hours a week. Moving gas bottles.
trade.story: A server in uniform wheels two heavy propane bottles across a wet courtyard in the rain at the start of a shift. And at the end. And the next day. Timestamped, repeating.
trade.insight: Portable gas heaters carry a labor cost as well as a purchase price, and trained hospitality staff are hard to find.
trade.argument: Every hour spent handling bottles is an hour off the floor. A fixed installation removes that recurring task, along with the manual handling that comes with it.
trade.channels: Trade press, LinkedIn, hospitality operations and WHS channels.
trade.audience: Operators, GMs, operations and WHS managers
trade.production: In Australia it also speaks to workplace health and safety, where manual handling is an active compliance topic. Keep it observational and never preachy.
trade.kpi: Commercial enquiry volume and rep conversations logged.
tones: Four hours a week. Moving gas bottles.
Two hundred hours a year of trained hospitality staff, moving cylinders.
She has wheeled the same two bottles across the same courtyard four hundred times.
It’s in nobody’s job description and it’s somebody’s whole shift.
trade.tone_note: Runs Deadpan or Dry only. The Absurd and Dark lines are kept for internal review and never run to the trade.
